topic: HL Regional Option: History of Asia & Oceania
subject: history

items.title: The Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961) was a CIA-trained failure
items.claim: What happened at the Bay of Pigs?

options.text: A successful US Marine landing in Cuba

Around 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles (Brigade 2506) landed at Bahía de Cochinos on 17 April 1961; without expected US air support, they were defeated within three days, with 114 killed and around 1,200 captured
A peaceful protest broken up by Castro's police

items.reveal:
The operation was planned under Eisenhower and inherited by Kennedy after his January 1961 inauguration. Kennedy cancelled the second air strike that would have neutralised Cuban air power. The exiles landed in swampy terrain with no popular uprising materialising.

Kennedy publicly accepted responsibility — 'success has many fathers, failure is an orphan' — and the CIA director Allen Dulles resigned. The prisoners were exchanged in December 1962 for $53 million of food and medicine.

The humiliation pushed Castro further toward the Soviet Union; Khrushchev's decision to place missiles in Cuba in 1962 followed directly. Operation Mongoose continued covert efforts against Castro through the 1960s.
items.why: Failed interventions can be more consequential than successful ones. The Bay of Pigs led directly to the Cuban Missile Crisis — and reshaped Cold War risk-taking for both sides.

items.title: Children under 10 worked underground in British coal mines until 1842
items.claim: What did the Mines Act of 1842 prohibit?

options.text: All child labour in the UK
Underground employment for women and girls, and for boys under 10 — following Lord Ashley's (later Shaftesbury) commission report with illustrations of children pulling coal trucks
Coal mining itself, switching the country to oil

items.reveal:
The 1842 Royal Commission report on children in mines included engravings of half-naked children — boys as young as 5 acting as 'trappers' opening ventilation doors, girls and women hauling coal in chains. The illustrations shocked Parliament.

The Act banned women and girls underground entirely and boys under 10. Earlier factory legislation (1819, 1833, 1844) limited child working hours and required schooling. Robert Owen's New Lanark mills (from 1800) had already shown a different model.
items.why: 'Reform' was driven partly by humanitarian shock and partly by middle-class anxiety about working-class women. The Acts solved one problem (underground child labour) without addressing others (above-ground work continued for decades).

items.title: Rosa Parks was a trained activist, not a tired seamstress
items.claim: Rosa Parks's December 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat is often told as a spontaneous act. What was her actual background?

options.text: She had no prior political involvement and acted purely on impulse
She was secretary of the Montgomery NAACP and had attended training at the Highlander Folk School months earlier
She was a paid organiser sent specifically to provoke an arrest
She was a member of the Communist Party, which is why she was arrested

items.reveal:
Parks had been Montgomery NAACP secretary since 1943. In summer 1955 she attended a workshop at Highlander Folk School in Tennessee on desegregation strategy. She was also not the first to refuse — Claudette Colvin had done the same in March 1955 but was 15, pregnant, and considered unsuitable as a test case by the NAACP.

Parks later wrote: 'People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.'
items.why: The 'tired seamstress' story makes civil rights feel like an accident of individual virtue. The actual story is one of organised, strategic activism — which is harder to teach but truer.
